answers.text: Every supplier email looks a little different, so I would say: always give exactly three lines, same order every time — delivery date, item and quantity, then any change from the original order. That way you get a summary that reads the same no matter which email it is.

For the claims, I would say list them with date, amount, category, submitter, in that order, one row each, and total the amount column at the end so it always comes from adding up the rows rather than someone typing a number in.

The problem is with the dates — call on the 14th, new date the 19th, but the text also says the 19th is 'three days out from today', and that does not add up since the 19th is five days after the 14th. The price part, 100 at 48.50 for 4,850, is fine.
62 up from 54 is close enough to 15%. The bit that is off is the on-time rate — 3 late out of 62 is nearer 95%, not the 97% written down.
I would sign off Output 2 — it shows the actual sales and returns figures, not just the 4.1%. Output 1 does not give you the numbers behind it, so there is nothing to check it against.

Reply 2 I would send as it is, since the order and credit references mean someone can look them up. Reply 1 is not automatically wrong, but the 'our error' claim and the credit cannot be checked without a reference, so someone would need to confirm those before it goes out too.
1. No, that is the customer's address. 2. Yes, it is just a total. 3. No, that has not gone out yet. 4. Yes, it is already on the website. 5. No, that number is not mine to share.

I would hold back the pricing and discount figures, and the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies. The delivery schedule I would be fine pasting in as it is, since there is nothing sensitive in dates and quantities on their own.

Before the weekly report goes out on Friday, I would cross-check the total deliveries figure against the depot log — that would catch it if a number came out wrong somewhere in the report, not just a spelling mistake.
I think step 1 is the one to watch, because if the AI reads the order wrong at the start, the rest of the steps just carry that mistake along.
